topic: steam wallpaper engine malware hijacks accounts
headline_marked: [[Malware hidden in Steam Wallpaper Engine]] hijacks accounts, downloaded tens of thousands of times
headline: Malware hidden in Steam Wallpaper Engine hijacks accounts, downloaded tens of thousands of times
summary: Kaspersky researchers found dozens of malicious packages, some downloaded over 10,000 times, spreading infostealers and ransomware since late last year.
details: Kaspersky researchers have uncovered a malware campaign operating on Steam since late last year, utilizing Wallpaper Engine to deploy credential stealers, crypto miners, and ransomware. The malicious packages, some downloaded tens of thousands of times before removal, hijack victim accounts to spread further infected files.

The attackers exploited Wallpaper Engine's "application wallpaper" feature, which allows standalone executable Windows programs to run as desktop backgrounds. This functionality created a pathway for third-party code to execute on users' machines, enabling the malware to operate discreetly.

Malware was delivered in two primary ways: either malicious EXE files, DLLs, or scripts were placed directly alongside legitimate wallpaper files, or payloads were hidden inside password-protected archives. These archives had passwords embedded in their names or JSON config files, allowing automated scripts to deploy the malware upon wallpaper application.

One analyzed sample from December showed a functional desktop game running while a DarkKomet backdoor (Synaptics.exe) and a tampered system library (AggregatorHost.dll) were dropped. This library located the running Steam app, stole account credentials, hijacked the live session, and transmitted data to a command-and-control server.

Control over active Steam sessions allowed attackers to post new malicious wallpapers under the victim's name, explaining the campaign's persistence despite takedowns. The majority of malicious download attempts (89%) were concentrated in China, followed by Russia, Singapore, and other regions, aligning with Wallpaper Engine's user base.

The payloads included DarkKomet, Lumma, Vidar infostealers, RenEngine loader, miners, and ransomware, suggesting multiple independent groups are leveraging this technique. This incident follows several other malware campaigns reaching players via Valve's storefront in recent years, including compromised game mods and titles.

topic: ai coding assistant turned computer into surveillance server
headline_marked: [[AI coding assistants create hidden surveillance logs]] of every interaction, including passwords and file paths
headline: AI coding assistants create hidden surveillance logs of every interaction, including passwords and file paths
summary: An investigation reveals that popular AI coding tools like Claude Code silently archive every user interaction, code snippet, and even system details locally, without explicit disclosure.
details: An investigation into AI coding assistants revealed that tools like Claude Code silently create extensive local logs of user interactions. These hidden files can contain every conversation, code snippet, file path, and even casually mentioned passwords.

The discovery was made when a user preparing to sell a laptop found 695 entries in Claude Code's config directory, totaling 43 MB of data. These logs capture not only user input but also AI responses and internal reasoning steps.

Beyond conversations, the logs also record every file operation—what was read, modified, or executed—and system information like the PATH, installed tools, and Java version. This data is stored in .jsonl files within project directories.

The article warns that this issue isn't exclusive to Claude Code, mentioning Cursor, Cline, and Windsurf as other tools that could exhibit similar behavior. Crucially, these files are easily recoverable with free software if a hard drive isn't thoroughly wiped.

The fundamental problem isn't the AI itself, but the undisclosed default behavior of these tools. Unlike web interfaces like ChatGPT or chat apps like WeChat, which make history logs visible, these local archives are generated without the user's knowledge or consent.

As AI coding tools become more powerful and ubiquitous, the article stresses that this lack of transparency regarding data archiving will not improve on its own. Users must be aware that their every interaction might be permanently stored.
caption:
